note.explanation: Atoms form bonds because combining can lower their energy and make them more stable. For example, sodium can lose one electron more easily than gain seven, while hydrogen can gain one electron to complete a duplet.
examples: Sodium loses one electron rather than gaining seven to complete its octet.
Hydrogen can gain one electron to complete its duplet.
note.checkAnswer: A duplet has 2 outer-shell electrons; an octet has 8.
note.simple: Atoms join with other atoms when doing so helps them become more stable.
note.checkQuestion: How many outer-shell electrons correspond to a duplet and an octet?
note.title: Why atoms form bonds
steps: Atoms can lower their energy by combining with other atoms.
A full outer shell is associated with stability: 2 electrons for a duplet or 8 for an octet.
Atoms may lose or gain electrons along an energetically easier path to reach this stable arrangement.
note.answer: Atoms form bonds to lower their energy and increase their stability.

options: To lower their energy and increase their stability
To increase the number of occupied shells
mcqs.stem: According to this section, why do atoms form chemical bonds?
rationales: This is correct: combining with other atoms can lower an atom’s energy and increase its stability.
This is incorrect: the section does not say that atoms bond to increase their number of occupied shells.
This is incorrect: bonding does not make an atom’s nucleus larger.
This is incorrect: bonding does not change an atom into a noble gas.

mcqs.stem: How many electrons are in the outermost shell of helium?
rationales: This is correct: helium has two electrons in its outermost shell.
This is incorrect: helium has two, not four, outermost-shell electrons.
This is incorrect: helium has two, not six, outermost-shell electrons.
This is incorrect: helium has two, not eight, outermost-shell electrons.

This is incorrect: seven electrons is not the number given for these noble gases.
This is correct: the other noble gases mentioned have eight electrons in their outermost shells.

mcqs.stem: What name was given to the principle that two electrons in the first shell or eight outermost-shell electrons mean stability?
rationales: This is correct: the section names this principle the Duplet or Octet Rule.

This is incorrect: the section does not use this name for the principle.
This is incorrect: this is not the name given in the section.

rationales: This is correct: the section says it is easier for sodium to lose one electron than to gain seven.

This is incorrect: the section describes sodium losing one electron, not seven.

This is incorrect: the section describes hydrogen changing by one electron, not losing two.
This is incorrect: the section discusses gaining one electron for hydrogen, not seven.

written.text: What type of elements lose their outer electron easily and what type of elements gain electron easily?
written.finalAnswer: Metals lose their outer electrons easily, while non-metals gain electrons easily.

steps.why: This compares the two paths the textbook describes for sodium and identifies the easier one.
steps.text: For sodium atom it is easy to lose one electron and stabilize itself than to gain seven electrons while completing its octet.

steps.why: This states the path sodium takes to form a bond.
steps.text: Sodium atom, therefore, adopts the energetically easier path and loses its electron to form a bond.

example.question: For sodium, which is the energetically easier path to stability: losing one electron or gaining seven electrons, and what does the atom do?
example.answer: Sodium loses one electron; it is energetically easier than gaining seven electrons.

explain.title: Atoms form bonds to become more stable
explain.body: Atoms have a tendency to decrease their energy. They can do this by combining with other atoms. This is a natural phenomenon because it increases the stability of atoms.

explain.title: The duplet and octet rule
explain.body: The textbook says: “having two electrons (for hydrogen and helium which have only the first shell) or eight electrons in the outermost shell meant stability and hence unreactivity as well. This principle was named as Duplet or Octet Rule.”

explain.title: Atoms can take an easier path
explain.body: An atom may lose or gain electrons to complete a duplet or octet. The textbook’s example is sodium: it is easier for sodium to lose one electron than to gain seven.

explain.title: Hydrogen can gain or lose one electron
explain.body: The textbook explains that hydrogen can lose one electron to become H⁺ or gain one electron to become H⁻; gaining one electron completes its duplet.

mistakes: Saying sodium gains seven electrons instead of stating that it loses one electron along the energetically easier path.
Mixing up the duplet and octet: a duplet has 2 electrons, while an octet has 8.
Writing that all atoms must follow the octet rule; the section says later investigations found the rule less important.
